title: The alphabet and spelling (Das Alphabet)
summary: Spell your name and understand spelled words. You will need it at every office, doctor's reception and phone call.
goals: Say the names of the German letters
Spell your name and email address
Ask someone to spell a word

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1: Welcome to A1 (Von A bis Z)

sections.title: Why spelling matters
sections.text: With a name like yours, people will ask you to spell it at the doctor's, at every office and on the phone. Most letter names follow the sounds from lesson 1. The table shows how each letter is **named**; press the speaker buttons and repeat.

The letters people mix up most are **E** and **I** (German E sounds like English 'eh', German I like English 'ee'), and **J**, **V**, **W**, **Y**, **Z**. Practise spelling your own name until these come out right.

sections.title: Spell these aloud, then press the speaker to check
rows: M, Ü, N, C, H, E, N
W, A, S, S, E, R

sections.title: On the phone
sections.text: Germans often spell with names on the phone: 'A wie Anton, B wie Berta'. The word 'wie' just means 'as in'. You don't need the list; the first letter of each name is what matters. For email addresses: @ is 'at' (said like English), a dot is 'Punkt', and a hyphen is 'Bindestrich'.

items.hint: A noun, so it starts with a capital letter.

items.question: You want someone to spell their name. What do you ask?

items.explanation: Wie schreibt man das? man = 'one' (people in general).

items.instruction: Spell your first name, your surname and the city you live in, letter by letter, using the German letter names (for example: ha, a, ypsilon, ka). Claude will check it.
items.prompt: Spell your first name, your surname and your city the German way.
